# Command crates, test phases, and the inputs that still fan out

This is the target design. [The source-graph report](modularization-design.md) supplies the exhaustive source inventory and cycle-edge classification. [The conservative command replay](modularization-command-replay.md) records the earlier, unsplit-test baseline. No production source, test assertion, enforcement setting, release target or frozen contract changes in this design task.

The binary dispatches each route to its command crate. A command owns its argument translation, typed verb, exit handling and command-only renderer. `cli-commands.json` is reconciled with the actual nested clap enums, rather than being a second unchecked command list. `target-moves.json` adds symbol moves to the source-derived graph: telemetry becomes run-metrics, flow state becomes flow-session, watcher protocol becomes watch-lease, and publication/observation debt become their own concepts. Branch-publication is shared by publish/recover/integrate; those commands do not import each other. Hidden retained execution calls run-control directly. The old command-shaped note and template-family buckets become planner-notes and plan-template: neither is a CLI route. The checker requires the command-crate set to equal the actual CLI routes, so neither creates a phantom command runner. Constructed argv is assigned through checked source mappings; only tests whose assertions prove parser/routing behavior remain against full-dispatch. Command-only functions in views and verbs move with their commands. The compatibility crate retains public module paths by re-exporting the identical items; it supplies no command implementation to an isolated runner.

Run-files is the common durable record IO and validated path boundary. It is also the fixture-writing boundary: an observation test need not launch a scheduler to obtain a historical run. It calls the real durable writers and schema validators to construct a valid precondition. Run-record retains typed records; run-projection folds recorded events; journal owns append/read behavior; planner-channel owns envelope/queue state; plan-edits owns accepted edits; publication owns branch lifecycle; task-store owns task-graph persistence; run-views owns shared snapshots, refresh, liveness and reading vocabulary. The generic YAML module belongs to yaml-codec, and branch template parsing/rendering belongs to branch-template; neither is collected in plan-model. The YAML module’s cross-document unit assertions move intact to a test-only integration project, so they do not create production codec-to-configuration edges. None is a miscellaneous core crate. Some dependencies are intentionally conservative unions of the current module's references; the graph is a design proof, not evidence that the future Rust packages compile.

The YAML rows in the original cycle table have the following target refinement. `yaml → filter`, `yaml → graph`, `yaml → maintenance`, `yaml → rules`, `yaml → taskgraph` and `yaml → templates` are seams owned by yaml-codec's **test-only** `DocumentCases` interface: a case supplies its real document loader and expected value, with adapters in the compatibility integration project. They retain real loader calls, not mock implementations. `yaml → error` and `yaml → sys` are genuinely shared diagnostics/process helpers used by those tests and move with that integration. The production codec's two generic functions reference none of these modules; the checker verifies that fact before moving the whole module. This replaces the earlier plan-model-owned provider proposal for those eight edges; it does not erase their assertions.

## Assertions and integrations

Manager ruling 205 authorizes separating setup assertions from consumer assertions. The schema-4 disposition catalog retains all 1,920 existing test functions. Each decomposed test has producer and consumer phases; each phase keeps the corresponding exit code, output and state assertions. Real shared writers build the next phase's precondition, including refusal/recovery states. Tests which assert live observer wakeup, ownership, takeover or control-to-driver ordering stay complete integrations. Their exact original IDs, participating commands and causal reason are enumerated below. The intent column includes an excerpt (up to 600 characters) of each test’s existing documentation, falling back to its descriptive name, so each retained sequence states the integration it proves. The catalog is an extraction specification: it does not claim these future Rust fixtures have already been implemented or benchmarked.

`phase-inputs.mjs` derives argv positions from the actual harness method signatures and follows scoped helper calls, imported helper bindings, fixture reads and runtime fake executables. It excludes helpers nested inside other tests and diagnostic-only failure dumps from command attribution. Literal argv forwarded through a helper is traced. `command-attributions.json` supplies reviewed mappings for constructed argv, external executables and assertion ownership; function and whole-module hashes refuse stale evidence, including changes to constants. Unreviewed argv refuses regeneration instead of silently becoming dispatcher coverage. `run_on` labels are not argv; `agentgraph_cmd` and `run_on_agentgraph` are traced to the actual onepipeline executable despite their legacy names. Only explicit parser/routing assertions retain the shipped dispatcher. Source hunk attribution charges both old and new declarations; unknown imports, impls or historical helpers conservatively retain the original file's consumers. This is a lexer-based conservative model, not Rust type resolution. During migration, compile failures reveal missing import moves; they must be fixed without dropping assertions or broadening command runners back to the facade.

All e2e functions requiring import/fixture changes are explicitly listed in the disposition table. Every decomposed row needs phase-local fixture construction; every isolated row needs the command runner and owner-crate imports. Every integration row keeps its command sequence and real subprocess boundary. Existing auxiliary suites remain in layout.json: public API/contract/parity tests deliberately keep the facade and the shipped binary, packaging tests keep the assembled real artifact, and credentialled journeys stay credentialled. Unit tests move with their owner items; a test referencing several command owners becomes an explicitly test-only integration and keeps each assertion. No production crate imports a test crate.

## Reproduce and interpret the estimates

```sh
node scripts/modularization/graph.mjs
node scripts/modularization/target-graph.mjs
node scripts/modularization/decompose.mjs
node scripts/modularization/target-replay.mjs "$ONEPIPELINE_NODE_SCRATCH_DIR/target-replay.json"
node scripts/modularization/target-report.mjs "$ONEPIPELINE_NODE_SCRATCH_DIR/target-replay.json"
just nx run onepipeline-modularization:check
```

The replay uses exactly 144 first-parent non-release PRs merged September 15 through October 15, 2026. The original source-graph snapshot is b0ce59cc40484264fe42adf27b89a32bd345be0e. Profile module weights remain the spike's 7a017fa local and dd2e5d6 CI snapshots. Today's profile reports 2.1% suite skipping; the earlier four-crate split reports 4.7% (the corrected replay is in the source-graph report). The conservative individual-test baseline committed at bffb01b3 reports 6.61%. These use different suite denominators. The target result below counts nonempty per-command runners and the retained integration/dispatch/public-API/support suites; it must be read beside test-seconds, not as a duration forecast.

Module seconds are divided equally across original tests and then equally across that test's phases. This conserves the measured module total but does not measure phase cost. Missing platform module weights are excluded and recorded in the replay JSON. Selection conservatively unions cfg branches on all platforms. Per-platform test-seconds differ because the measured weights differ, not because tests were removed on Windows.

The replay compares each crate's reachable package records in both locks, including version, source, checksum and dependency edges. Unknown modern roots absent from historical locks select their consumers conservatively and are named in the output; the public resolver refuses unknown roots. Ambiguous package versions are included conservatively. This is package-resolution projection, not Cargo feature/target resolution. Manifest requirements are projected by each crate's external roots; edition, Rust version, profile, resolver and feature changes retain their actual shared scope. Python 3.11+ stdlib tomllib parses the TOML. Comments/order in the compiler pin do not change a fingerprint; a changed uniform Rust channel really changes every Rust crate. No private substitute for a sibling ConfigRef, MergePolicy or Transcript type is invented to hide a genuine dependency. A suite that builds or uses a subprocess double retains the real onepipeline-testfakes package resolution and its library/manifest inputs; runtime executables do not become dependency-free merely because the runner invokes them out of process.

Before Nx selection, migration must materialize the fingerprints into owned projection projects and declare each consuming crate's dependency on its projection. Raw lockfile/toolchain entries must then leave shared named inputs. The test builds a real scratch Git/Nx workspace and commits command, transitive shared, lock and compiler changes, proving exact suite equality with Nx's affected selection. This task changes no live Nx Rust invalidation rule. The broad-PR table below names every historical PR still selecting more than half; resolved input paths and exact source hunks are retained in replay JSON.

Compile estimates use the spike's Linux nine-runner prototype: 574→795 cold CPU seconds and 193→264 incremental CPU seconds. The generated table applies linear extra-link stress to this design's nonempty runner count. Its macOS and Windows scenarios scale historical cached wall baselines by that Linux ratio: they are uncalibrated scenarios, not benchmarks, bounds or promised compile savings. Local run F took 10,293.5 seconds under shared-host load. Multiplying that test phase by estimated skipped seconds assumes proportional scheduling, excludes compilation/lint/other gate work and does not establish a measured gate speedup. The present evidence does not establish the 30-minute goal; that limitation was sent to the manager as c-6953a04a0f80fd84810e253effc6c16a. It does not justify sharding, sampling or weakening coverage.

## Land one boundary at a time

The first migration row combines render-cost with the fingerprint materializer/Nx projection dependencies and phase-local test input/support projects, retaining the current suite as the parity oracle. Its skip share includes avoiding unrelated lock/pin invalidation and selecting independently owned test inputs; it is not all attributable to that leaf crate. Next extract the remaining leaf data/IO concepts and re-export their exact public types; then extract command adapters/renderers and move their phases one command at a time. The generated migration table gives the skip share after each named extraction, retaining residual-package dependencies until a runner's complete closure is available. It is deliberately not a sum of independent best cases. Shared protocol changes still run their consumers at every stage.

For every row: preserve clap defaults/help/exit codes and the exact stdout/stderr contract by the existing compiled-binary/parity assertions; preserve type identity through re-exports rather than new wrappers; retain serialized versions/goldens unchanged; move every listed assertion before removing its original container; keep live integrations intact. Publish implementation packages and facade in lockstep only under the approved packaging plan; this task makes no publication change. The canonical template asset moves to plan-template; the facade source archive must continue carrying it through a generated package copy with a drift check, rather than maintaining two editable templates. Each step must pass its real Rust compilation and existing tests before landing. The design graph's acyclicity does not substitute for those future checks.

## Local verification scope

Planner reply 214 confirms that this design-only dispatch owes the research project's checks and judged diff lint locally. Current Nx docs/scripts globs additionally select `onepipeline`, `pool-maintenance`, `onepipeline-contract`, `onepipeline-e2e` and `onepipeline-npm`; their gating journeys remain with the change request's required checks. `onepipeline-visual-docs` is also selected but remains advisory under the repository's existing policy. No live input, test command, coverage threshold or enforcement rule changes here.

## Target replay

The original 1,273 cross-command assignments partition as support: 72; library: 11; integration: 311; isolated: 138; decompose: 736; dispatch: 5. All 1920 original tests remain represented below.

## Baseline beside the target

The 6.61% unsplit-test baseline is committed at bffb01b3. Suite denominators differ (31 baseline versus the target count below); both seconds columns allocate the same observed module totals and are estimates, not new timings.

| Platform | Baseline suite runs skipped | Baseline estimated seconds skipped | Target suite runs skipped | Target estimated seconds skipped |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| local | 6.61% | 2.53% | 8.30% | 5.10% |
| linux | 6.61% | 2.55% | 8.30% | 5.00% |
| macos | 6.61% | 2.57% | 8.30% | 4.95% |
| windows | 6.61% | 2.69% | 8.30% | 4.97% |


## Command replay output

1920 existing tests, 3638 assertion-preserving command phases, 43 nonempty suites, 144 historical PRs. Empty command runners are excluded from the savings denominator. Test-second figures below are estimates obtained by dividing each measured module's seconds equally among its tests; they are not per-test measurements. Missing timings are excluded, never zero-duration observations.

| Platform | Suite runs skipped | Estimated observed test-seconds skipped | Observed module-seconds/full run |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| local | 8.30% | 5.10% | 36620 |
| linux | 8.30% | 5.00% | 10409 |
| macos | 8.30% | 4.95% | 13333 |
| windows | 8.30% | 4.97% | 37567 |

Estimated compile stress scenario (not a benchmark or a confidence interval):

| Job | Baseline | All-runner stress estimate | Delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Linux | 574 cold CPU s | 1734.3 CPU s | +1160.3 CPU s |
| macOS | 233 cached wall s | 704.0 wall s | +471.0 wall s |
| Windows, each leg | 106–164 cached wall s | 320.3–495.5 wall s | +214.3–331.5 wall s |

Linux incremental all-source CPU stress estimate: 193 → 565.8 s. Local test-phase scenario: 10,293.5 × 5.10% = 524.7 wall seconds avoided on average if concurrency and scheduling stayed proportional; this excludes compilation and every other gate phase. There is no measured local gate speedup.

## Every PR still selecting more than half

The named inputs below are the actual changed inputs whose union forces selection. Manifest edits are projected by each crate's actual external roots, with shared edition/profile/resolver/features affecting their real consumers. The current single compiler pin really changes all Rust consumers; modularization alone cannot remove that dependency. Shared source edits can be narrowed only by moving the referenced DTO/helper or command fragment out of that source file; changing an actually shared wire type still reaches its consumers. Splitting borrowed test helpers removes whole-module attribution, but none is silently dropped here. Nx/recipe/config changes remain global. For rows without an individually broad input, the union of the listed narrower edits crosses half; no single-input design change eliminates that union.

## Command-suite migration replay

Every extraction preserves the facade's public paths and type identities through re-exports, keeps the shipped dispatcher routing to the production command entry point, and moves the listed tests with unchanged assertions. Until a runner and all its dependency crates land, its tests still link the residual package. The compatibility facade and cross-command suite remain on the complete graph. Lock projections are not usable in Nx until the materialization hook and explicit projection-project dependencies land; these rows assume that prerequisite, described above.

## What narrowing the docs/scripts globs frees

Holding this proposed 43-suite graph fixed, 83 of the 144 PRs edit docs/ or scripts/. Retaining blanket docs/** and scripts/** inputs selects every suite for those edits. Replacing those blanket inputs with each suite's actual fixture/script inputs frees at least one suite on **12 PRs**; **1** of those can skip all suites. It removes **104 suite runs** across the cohort. Suite-run skipping is 6.62% with blanket inputs and 8.30% with the proposed inputs. This isolates the glob effect on the same graph; it is not a claim that today's single binary already has the proposed isolation. Required real fixture inputs remain.

## Every original test and retained integration

Each row preserves all assertions. Decomposed rows move setup exit/output assertions to the producer's phase and consumer assertions to the consumer's phase over records written by the real production writers. Failure fixtures use the same envelope/schema validators and durable writers. Retained integrations exercise the listed commands in the original sequence, with the live ordering in the reason. full-dispatch retains parser/routing assertions against the shipped binary; public-api retains facade identity/parity assertions. Shared helper imports and fixture paths are explicit runner inputs in the replay JSON.

The double answers each reading at the argv a caller sends: with no `--format`, and with `--format text`, one line per event in the core's own text view — the agent's reasoning and words beside its tool call — then the text report; under `--format json` the event envelopes, `reasoning`, `t | The real support subprocess/fixture boundary is the subject; keep these assertions in test-support rather than a production command suite.
